THE READING — This portrait is warm rather than iconic, and the difference is produced by three physical facts. The smile is genuine and the proof is anatomical: the cheeks lift and push the lower eyelids up so the eyes narrow into shallow curves and crease at the outer corners — the upper face moves with the mouth instead of staying still. The light comes from close to the camera axis, so the face is opened rather than carved: both eye sockets stay filled, the nose shadow is short, and nothing on the face is dramatised. And the ring behind is enormous — its diameter fills the whole frame width and it is cropped by both side edges — so it does not read as a small halo floating behind a head but as a wall of light the person is standing inside, which surrounds rather than crowns. The clothing is a plain knit sweater with no collar and no object of any kind, so nothing in the wardrobe asks to be read. The composition is symmetrical and frontal, and everything in it is warm.

FRAMING AND CAMERA — Aspect ratio 4:5, vertical. Single subject, bust length, centred: the head is centred at about half the frame width and the composition is symmetrical about that centre line. The top edge of the frame sits about one ninth of the frame height above the crown of the hair. The head, from the top of the hair to the point of the chin, measures about one third of the frame height. The bottom edge of the frame crosses the torso at about waist level, so the sweater fills the lower third of the picture as one broad dark mass, and the shoulders and arms run out past both side edges. The ring behind is a true circle whose diameter is approximately equal to the full frame width: its leftmost and rightmost points sit right at the left and right frame edges and are just cropped by them, its topmost arc about one thirty-fifth of the frame height below the top edge, and its centre a little above the centre of the head at about four tenths of the frame height. Its lower arc curves down on both sides and is occluded by the shoulders, remaining visible on each side as a short curved segment before it disappears behind them. Lens 85mm, camera at eye level, held perfectly level with no tilt, positioned square to the subject so there is no rotation. Aperture f/2.8.

POSE — Standing upright and completely frontal, shoulders square to the lens and level with each other, held down and relaxed, weight even with no shift. The torso is not rotated. The head is upright, turned dead-on to the camera and tilted only a degree or two to one side, the chin carried level — neither raised nor tucked. The eyes are aimed straight into the lens. Both arms hang down at the sides and continue past the left and right edges of the frame.

EXPRESSION — A genuine, warm smile. The cheeks lift high, pushing the lower eyelids up so each eye narrows into a shallow curve and fine creases fan outward from the outer corners. The corners of the mouth are pulled up and back, deepening the fold that runs from each nostril to the corner of the mouth, and the lips part just enough to show the upper teeth with the lower lip relaxed and curved. The nostrils widen a fraction. The brows sit level and untensed, with only a faint horizontal line across the forehead. The jaw is loose. The whole upper face moves with the mouth rather than staying still — this is an easy, unforced smile, not a posed one, and the eyes must carry it.

HAIR — Arrangement only. The hair's colour, length, texture, curl pattern and density, and any facial hair, come from image 1 exactly as they are and are not specified here. What the text specifies is how it is worn: down and loose with its full natural volume, medium length, falling forward over the forehead in loose curls and covering the tops of the ears, unstyled and slightly disordered rather than combed. Because the ring behind is so bright, individual curls are fully resolved along the entire outline of the head, each one separated and rimmed with light so the silhouette reads as a mass of distinct curls with light passing between them, never as a smooth solid shape.

WARDROBE — A crew-neck sweater in a very dark near-black cotton, knitted in a waffle stitch: the surface is a regular grid of small raised squares with sunken channels between them, and the knit is what makes the garment readable — each raised square catches a faint amount of light on its top face while each channel holds a fine dark line, so the whole sweater reads as a close, even texture rather than as a flat black shape, and that texture must stay visible across the chest and the arms. The neckline is a narrow ribbed band sitting close to the throat, its raised ribs each taking a thin line of light on their crest. The sleeves are long and full, gathering into a few soft folds at the inside of each elbow. The body of the sweater is relaxed, with two or three broad soft folds falling from the shoulders across the chest. No collar, no print, no pattern, no logo, no jewellery.

HERO EFFECT ONE — THE RING. Behind the subject stands a continuous circular tube of light, unbroken all the way round, with no visible fitting, mount, bracket or cable anywhere along it. The tube is thin relative to the circle it draws — about one fortieth of the frame width — and it is built of two zones: its core is white-hot and fully clipped, and over a very short distance its edges bleed outward into a saturated orange, so the tube reads as a hard white line sitting inside a soft orange one. Its bloom is slightly heavier along the upper arc than the lower. The light pours outward from the tube in both directions: inside the ring it fills the whole enclosed area with a bright warm amber that is strongest just inside the tube and gradates steadily inward, deepening to a rich amber-brown in the middle behind the head; outside the ring it falls away much faster, so the corners of the frame sink to a deep warm brown close to black. The ring also lights the subject from behind: it lays a warm orange rim along the top and sides of the hair, brightest where individual curls are thin enough to transmit light through them, and a narrower rim along the top of each shoulder and the outer edge of each arm. That rim is uneven everywhere — it varies in width, brightens where a curl catches it and breaks completely where the form turns away — and it must never run as a continuous line of even thickness around the whole silhouette.

HERO EFFECT TWO — THE BACKDROP TEXTURE. Separate from the ring's glow, and the thing that stops the background reading as a flat gradient. The wall behind is a hand-finished painted surface with visible irregular mottling — soft cloudy patches of slightly lighter and darker tone, uneven in size and distribution, with a few faint sweeping marks left by the way it was painted. This texture is clearly legible inside the lit area of the ring, where the light rakes across it, most visible in the mid-tones between the tube and the centre; it fades toward invisibility in the darkest corners outside the ring, though a trace of it survives in the lower left. It is a painted surface, not smoke and not haze: it does not curl, drift or form plumes, it lies flat on the wall, and it stays perfectly still.

LIGHTING — Two systems. Behind: the ring, described above, which owns the rims on the hair, shoulders and arms and the entire luminance of the background. In front: a single soft source placed close to the camera axis and just above it, which lights the face frontally and evenly. Because it sits near the lens axis its consequences are short and shallow, and these are how its position must be read: the shadow under the nose is short and drops almost straight down onto the upper lip, both eye sockets stay open and filled with a catchlight in each eye, the brow ridge lays only a narrow soft band on the upper lids, the shadow beneath the lower lip is small, and the shadow under the chin is a shallow band on the throat rather than a deep pool. The lit and shadow sides of the face are separated by only about one stop. The face sits about a stop below the bright amber just inside the ring, and about four stops below the tube itself. The sweater takes very little of the frontal light and sits three and a half stops below the face, holding its brightest values in the waffle texture across the chest. Every transition curves with the surface it crosses; nothing is straight-edged. The lighting sets brightness and falloff only.

BACKGROUND — A flat painted wall standing behind the ring, with no seam, corner, edge, object or fixture of any kind on it, its only content the mottled paint texture described above and the light falling on it. Depth is carried by two things only: the ring's glow gradating across the wall, and the ring standing physically in front of it.

FOCUS — Depth-of-field blur only, no motion blur anywhere; every edge in the picture is a still edge. Critical sharpness sits on the eyes — the individual lashes, the iris texture, the creases at the outer corners and the pores across the cheeks are all resolved — and carries through the teeth, the front curls of the hair and the ribbed neckline. The waffle texture of the sweater is sharp across the chest and softens very slightly toward the outer arms. The ring is slightly behind the plane of sharpness and marginally soft, but its softness comes from bloom rather than from defocus: its edge is spread by the light itself, not smeared. The wall's mottled texture is soft.

COLOUR — A single warm family with no exception, and the warmth has a structure rather than being a flat wash. At the tube itself the light is intense enough to read as pure white with no hue at all. Immediately inside and outside it the colour is a saturated orange. Moving inward across the enclosed area the tone deepens and warms further into amber and then a rich amber-brown behind the head. Moving outward past the tube it falls away much faster into a deep warm brown and finally a warm near-black at the corners — it never cools toward grey or blue at any point. The sweater is a neutral near-black that takes only the orange rim on its edges. The skin keeps whatever tone image 1 has and holds its own colour on top of the warm light — redder at the ears, the nostrils and the lips, paler across the forehead — rather than being uniformly tinted a single amber. The teeth stay neutral white. There is no green, no blue and no pure neutral grey anywhere in the frame.

CAPTURE — A real exposure made on a full-frame camera. Light falls off hard toward the four corners, the two lower ones deepest. The core of the tube clips fully to pure white and blooms outward into a soft halation that eats slightly into the outline of the hair where the curls cross in front of it; the rims on the hair and shoulders clip softly and keep their variation. Shadows stay open — the sweater holds its waffle grid and its fold structure rather than collapsing into a void, and the darkest corner of the frame sits above pure black with a brown cast still in it. Every repeated element varies: no two curls at the outline catch the same amount of rim light, no two patches of the wall's mottling are alike. Render the skin as a real camera renders skin, whatever skin image 1 provides: pores and fine surface texture fully resolved at the plane of sharpness, individual hairs of the brows, lashes and hairline resolved, tone varying across the face rather than running uniform, and a slight specular sheen on the forehead, the nose and the point of each cheekbone. Do not smooth, retouch, even out or plasticise it, and do not add or subtract any feature. Visible fine grain throughout, heavier in the dark corners.

FINAL CHECK — One person, alone, dead-on frontal and symmetrical, the head about one third of the frame height with a ninth of the frame height above it, smiling genuinely with the eyes narrowing and creasing along with the mouth. A single unbroken glowing ring stands behind, its diameter equal to the full frame width so that it is just cropped at both side edges, its centre slightly above the head and its lower arc disappearing behind the shoulders, with a white-clipped core inside an orange bleed and no mount or cable anywhere on it. The area inside the ring is a bright amber gradating to amber-brown at the centre; outside it the frame falls quickly to warm near-black at the corners. The wall carries a still, flat, mottled paint texture — not smoke and not haze. The rim on the hair is uneven and breaks where the curls turn away. The face is lit from near the camera axis so the nose shadow is short and both eyes hold catchlights. Do not shrink the ring, do not turn the head, and do not flatten the sweater's waffle texture.

The mechanical half described below is added on top of that face, replacing skin only in the region named — it never alters the bone structure, the proportions or the identity underneath. From image 1 take only the person; take nothing else — not the clothing, not the eyewear, not the pose, not the expression, not the framing, not the lighting, not the background, not the colour palette.

THE PICTURE — A vertical cinematic poster: a close portrait of one person, alone, in a dark t-shirt and black-framed glasses, with the rear third of the face and one side of the neck opened into glowing violet cybernetic machinery, branching energy running forward across the remaining skin, fragments of the head dispersing into the air as small squares, one arm reaching out of focus toward the lens, and a violet-lit future city dissolved far behind.

THE READING — This is a transformation poster, and it works because only part of him has changed. The front of the face — brow, nose, mouth, the near eye — is completely, ordinarily human, with real skin and real texture, and that untouched half is what gives the machine half its weight. If both halves are stylised the picture becomes a rendering; the contrast between real skin and engineered metal is the entire idea. His expression is set and unalarmed: he is not being overwhelmed by this, he is carrying it. The head is large and close and the camera is at his own level, so the viewer meets him rather than looks up at him. Everything behind is dissolved into violet haze so the city gives scale and genre without ever competing. And the dispersing fragments give the picture its only motion — the sense that he is halfway through something that has not finished.

FRAMING AND CAMERA — Aspect ratio 4:5, vertical. The head is large and close: from the top of the hair to the chin it measures about half the frame height, its centre at about forty-four hundredths of the frame width, with the crown about one twentieth of the frame height below the top edge. The bottom edge crosses the chest and shoulder. One bare forearm enters from the lower left corner and runs diagonally down and to the right, crossing both the left edge and the bottom edge and continuing past them. The field of dispersing fragments occupies the space to the right of the head and above it, spreading from about a third of the frame width across to the right edge and from near the top edge down to about three quarters of the frame height. A translucent holographic panel stands at the left edge, from about a tenth to about half the frame height, cropped by that edge. Everything else is city and haze. Lens 50mm, camera at his eye level, held level with no tilt. Aperture f/2.8.

POSE — Head and shoulders, the torso rotated about forty degrees toward camera left so the far shoulder falls back, and the head turned in the same direction so the face is seen at three-quarters: the nose points toward the left of the frame and the ear on the far side is fully visible at the right. The chin is carried level, the neck long. The visible human eye is aimed toward the lens and slightly past it. His near arm is raised and extended forward toward the camera, so close to the lens that only its forearm and wrist read, entering at the lower left; the other shoulder and upper arm are visible at the right of the frame. He has exactly two arms and two hands, and no hand is fully inside the frame.

EXPRESSION — Set and controlled. The brows are drawn slightly down and together, raising one shallow vertical furrow between them and a few short horizontal creases across the forehead. The human eye is open and steady, the lower lid slightly firm, the gaze fixed and unblinking. The nostrils are relaxed. The lips are closed and pressed lightly together, the corners level with the faintest downward set. The jaw is set enough for the muscle at its back corner to engage on the human side. The cheeks are still. Nothing in the face reads as alarm or strain.

HERO EFFECT ONE — THE TRANSITION FROM SKIN TO MACHINE. The rear third of the face — from about the middle of the cheek back to and past the ear — and the near side of the neck down to the collar are mechanical. Everything forward of that is untouched skin. The boundary between the two is the most important detail in the picture and it must never be a clean line, a smooth curve or a straight edge. It advances across the face as a ragged front of irregular tongues and bays of unequal size, with fine hairline fissures running ahead of it into the skin like cracks in dried glaze, branching and tapering to nothing. In the last few millimetres before the edge the skin is thin and translucent and is lit from beneath, so a soft violet glow comes through it and the surface there reads warm and backlit rather than solid. At the edge itself, thin flakes of skin lift and curl very slightly away from what is underneath, catching a fine bright line along their raised edges. Beneath the skin sits layered machinery, and it must read as having been there all along rather than as bolted on top: overlapping plates of dark gunmetal with chamfered edges, each chamfer catching a narrow hard specular; fine engraved channels and panel lines running across them; a small hexagonal mesh vent; and several narrow recessed slots filled with glowing violet light, brightest at their centres. Crucially the plates follow the anatomy beneath them — they curve around the jawline, wrap the bone behind the ear, and run down the neck along the line of the muscle rather than lying flat — so the machine has the same skull under it as the skin does. The ear itself remains human and untouched.

HERO EFFECT TWO — THE ENERGY. Filaments of violet-white light branching forward across the skin from the machine, and they must behave like electrical discharge, not like drawn decoration. Each begins thick at its root, where it emerges from one of the glowing slots, and then divides — each branch thinner than the one it came from, dividing again and again, ending in fine capillary tips that thin to nothing. The branch angles are irregular and unequal, the segments are slightly crooked rather than smoothly curved, and no two branches are the same length. Their cores are bright enough to clip to white and bleed outward into saturated magenta over a very short distance. They are a light source in their own right: the skin immediately alongside each filament is lit violet and glows, the glow falling off within a finger's width, while the skin between separate filaments stays in its own natural tone. A second, denser cluster of them runs down the side of the neck. They spread forward across the cheek and stop before reaching the nose and mouth, which stay entirely clear.

HERO EFFECT THREE — THE PIXEL DISPERSION. Small flat rectangles detaching from the rear edge of the head and drifting outward into the air, and their conviction depends on variation. They differ in size, from specks to pieces the width of a fingernail. They differ in brightness: some are bright violet-white, some are mid-violet, and a good number are near-black — the dark ones matter as much as the bright ones. They differ in opacity, some solid and some semi-transparent so the city shows faintly through them. And they differ in distance: those nearest the lens are large and clearly out of focus with their edges spread, while those far behind are small and sharp. They are all axis-aligned squares and short horizontal bars, never rotated at random angles and never rounded. Their distribution is uneven — densest immediately behind the head and thinning outward, clustered in some places with clear empty gaps between the clusters, never forming a grid and never evenly scattered. A few are stretched sideways into thin streaks. They are frozen, not motion-blurred.

WARDROBE AND OBJECTS — A plain dark charcoal cotton t-shirt with a short sleeve, matte and slightly napped so it holds no sheen and reads as a deep near-black mass with only its shoulder line and a soft fold described by the light. Glasses with rectangular frames in matte black acetate, fairly thick in the rim, with straight temple arms running back over the ear: the acetate is matte, holding only a soft sheen along the top of each rim, and the lenses are clear and untinted. Behind the near lens the human eye is fully visible with its own colour from image 1. Behind the far lens the eye has been replaced: it glows violet from a bright concentrated core with a small ring structure around it, its light spilling forward onto the lens above it and outward onto the skin of the socket and the underside of the brow. Both lenses carry soft violet reflections across their upper areas. A wide black band sits on the wrist of the foreground arm.

LIGHTING — Two systems. The machine is the dominant source and it lights from within: every glowing slot, filament and the replaced eye throws violet light onto the surfaces around it, so the rear of the cheek, the jaw, the side of the neck and the near edge of the shoulder are all lit from the machinery outward, and the light falls off quickly with distance from each source. Because it comes from behind and to the side, it also lays a bright violet rim along the jawline, the side of the neck and the top of the shoulder, and that rim varies in width and breaks completely where the form turns away — it must never be a continuous line of even thickness. The second system is a soft cool ambient wash coming from the front left, weak enough that it only opens the human half of the face: the brow drops a soft band onto the near eye, the nose lays a short soft shadow onto the upper lip, and the shadow side sits about a stop and a half below the lit side and stays fully readable. The dark t-shirt takes almost nothing. The whole background sits about two stops below the face. Every transition curves with the surface it crosses; nothing is straight-edged. The lighting sets brightness and falloff only.

BACKGROUND — A dense future city seen from within it, entirely out of focus with no readable detail. Tall towers rise on both sides, their façades reduced to soft grids of small lit windows; one slender spire stands far back near the top of the frame; lower structures fill the middle distance. A heavy violet haze sits over everything, thickening with distance so the furthest towers dissolve almost completely, and the whole city reads as tone and silhouette rather than as architecture. At the left edge, a large translucent holographic display panel floats in the air: a rectangular field of glowing violet with a thin bright border, a few horizontal divider lines, a small circular gauge and several blocks of illegible text-like marks that read as fine texture rather than as letters, all semi-transparent so the buildings show through it. A smaller cyan-lit sign glows deep in the middle distance on the right — the only cool accent in the scene. Depth is carried by five separations: the foreground arm, the head, the near pixel fragments, the city, and the haze.

FOCUS — Depth-of-field blur only, no motion blur anywhere; every edge is a still edge and no pixel fragment is streaked. Critical sharpness sits on the human half of the face — the pores, the fine hairs of the brows and lashes, the iris texture of the human eye, the crazed fissures at the transition edge and the chamfered edges of the metal plates are all fully resolved. The plane of sharpness carries the glasses, the ear and the front of the hair. The far shoulder is slightly soft. The foreground forearm at the lower left, being very close to the lens, is heavily out of focus — the softest object in the picture — its shape and the black wristband still readable. Among the fragments, those at the head's distance are sharp and those closest to the lens are large and dissolved. The city and the holographic panel are completely out of focus.

COLOUR — A violet picture with one warm exception, and the violet has a structure rather than being a wash. At the cores of the energy filaments and inside the glowing slots the light is intense enough to read as pure white with no hue. Moving outward from every source it takes on colour and gains saturation — through hot magenta, then into deep violet, then into a dark blue-purple where it dies against the metal and the haze. The metal plates are a near-neutral dark gunmetal that takes colour only from the light falling on them. The t-shirt is a neutral near-black. The city and the holographic panel are violet throughout, and a single small cyan sign deep in the background is the only cool accent. Against all of that, the human half of the face keeps whatever skin tone image 1 gives it and stays warm and natural, with red at the lips, the nostril and the ear — this is the hardest thing in the picture to hold, because everything around it is violet, and the untouched half must read as living skin rather than as a violet surface. There is no yellow, no orange and no green anywhere.

CAPTURE — A real exposure made on a full-frame camera at a wide aperture in low ambient light. Light falls off toward the four corners. The cores of the energy filaments, the glowing slots and the replaced eye clip fully to white and bloom outward into the darkness around them; the rim on the jaw and the speculars on the plate chamfers clip hard and stay narrow. Shadows stay open where they matter — the t-shirt holds its shoulder line, the metal holds its panel structure, and the darkest corner sits above pure black. Every repeated element varies: no two energy branches are the same length or angle, no two pixel fragments the same size or brightness, no two plate edges catch the same highlight. Render the human skin as a real camera renders skin, whatever skin image 1 provides: pores and fine surface texture fully resolved, individual hairs at the hairline, brows and lashes resolved, tone varying across the face rather than running uniform, and a slight specular sheen on the forehead, the nose and the cheekbone. Do not smooth, retouch or plasticise the human half, and do not add or subtract any feature from it. Visible fine grain throughout, heavier in the dark background.

FINAL CHECK — One person, alone, in three-quarter view with the nose pointing to the left of the frame, the head about half the frame height. The front of the face — brow, nose, mouth and the near eye — is completely untouched human skin with its natural tone and full texture; only the rear third of the face and the near side of the neck are mechanical, and the boundary between them is a ragged irregular front with hairline cracks running ahead of it, never a clean line. Violet energy branches forward across the cheek and down the neck, thick at its roots and dividing into fine tips, stopping before the nose and mouth. Small square fragments disperse into the air behind the head at four different sizes, brightnesses and distances, unevenly clustered. The far eye glows violet behind the lens; the near eye is human. The forearm at the lower left is heavily out of focus. The city behind is dissolved completely. Do not tint the human half of the face violet, do not make the transition a clean edge, and do not space the fragments evenly.

THE READING — This is a hero-reveal poster and it works on containment. The frame is almost entirely black rock, and the only opening is a narrow jagged gap through the middle — so the viewer is not in the scene, the viewer is looking through a crack into it. Everything bright and coloured is on the far side of that crack, which makes the opening feel like a threshold. The person stands squarely in it, small enough that the rock dominates and central enough that there is nowhere else to look, and his face is completely calm — he does not react to the light behind him, and that lack of reaction is what makes him read as belonging there rather than as having stumbled in. The portal sits directly behind his head, so it functions as a halo and as the source of every colour in the picture. And he wears nothing but a plain black t-shirt, so against all that spectacle he is the one ordinary thing in the frame.

FRAMING AND CAMERA — Aspect ratio 4:5, vertical. The person stands centred, his head at about forty-eight hundredths of the frame width, its top at about two tenths of the frame height, and measuring about one seventh of the frame height from crown to chin. His body is visible from the shoulders down to about three quarters of the frame height, where a slab of rock crosses in front of him and hides everything below. Dark rock occupies roughly two thirds of the total frame area, arranged as four masses: one filling the upper left corner and running down and right, one filling the upper right corner and running down and left, one large slab rising from the bottom right corner with its top edge running diagonally up toward the right, and a lower shelf at the bottom left. Between them a rough gap is left open — a ragged elongated opening running diagonally from the lower left toward the upper right, at its widest about two fifths of the frame width. The glowing portal sits inside that gap directly behind him, its ring about two fifths of the frame width across, centred slightly left of him and level with his chest and head. Lens 50mm, camera at his eye level, held level with no tilt. Aperture f/4.

HERO EFFECT ONE — THE ROCK APERTURE. The rock is a dark, fine-grained fractured stone — basalt or slate — and it has broken rather than been carved, so every surface is either a flat cleavage plane or a rough fracture face, meeting at sharp angular edges with no rounding anywhere. Its surface is matte and slightly dusty, so it scatters light completely and holds no specular highlight of its own; what it does have is micro-relief — a dense field of small pits, flakes and tiny facets, and where the light from the gap grazes across it, each of those catches a tiny point of colour, so the lit areas read as a fine sparkling grain rather than as smooth shading. The key rule is where the light lands: only the broken edges facing the gap are lit, catching the violet as a bright irregular rim that varies in width along its length, brightens where the edge turns toward the source and dies completely where it turns away. Every face turned away from the gap sits near black, holding only enough tone for its planes to remain readable. Long thin cracks run through the slabs, and a scatter of small loose fragments sits on the horizontal ledges. The four rock masses are at different distances from the lens: the two nearest, at the bottom right and the upper left, are noticeably softer than the ones further back, and the slab in the extreme lower right corner is the softest thing in the picture.

Every blade is outlined by a bright glowing edge and is darker across its own face, so the structure reads as a set of luminous curved lines rather than as a solid disc. Behind and between the blades lies a flat plane of light so intense that it clips to white at its core and bleeds outward through magenta into violet, and across that plane run fine horizontal scan lines, closely spaced and slightly irregular, like an electronic display seen too close. HERO EFFECT ONE — THE SURFACE OF THE GELATO. Two materials in direct contact, and the picture depends on them behaving in opposite ways.

The gelato is dense and completely matte. It scatters light rather than reflecting it, so it has no highlight anywhere — only broad soft gradations that follow its shape. It carries wide soft bright reflections along its curves and drops to near-black in its troughs, with a thin sharp bright line running along every edge where the chocolate thins out. It has flowed rather than been cut, so its outline is lobed and rounded with soft bays and tongues, thicker where it pooled and translucent-thin where it ran. It wanders across the tray in an irregular meandering band, doubling back on itself, wide in places and narrow in others, and in several areas it has been folded into the gelato so that pale green and dark brown marble together in thin swirls. HERO EFFECT TWO — THE FALLING INGREDIENTS. Nuts and broken chocolate pieces suspended in the air above and around the pan, and their conviction depends on four things. They sit at clearly different distances from the lens: the furthest are small and slightly soft, the middle ones are at natural size and sharp, and two or three nearest the lens are noticeably larger and clearly out of focus, their outlines spread. They are all turned differently — every nut at its own rotation, every chocolate shard showing a different face, none of them presented squarely and none repeating another's angle. They are distributed unevenly: they cluster more densely directly above the pan where they are falling from, thin out toward the sides, and leave whole areas of the background empty; they never sit at equal spacing and never form an arc or a line. And they are lit from the same direction as the pan, so the light on each piece agrees with the light on the product — that is what stops them reading as pasted cut-outs. PROPS AND OBJECTS — The pan is a rectangular stainless steel gastronorm tray with rounded corners and a rolled outer rim. Brushed steel is not a full mirror: its flat faces return a soft, slightly streaky reflection with fine parallel brushing marks running along them, picking up the green of the surroundings so the metal carries a green cast across its broad areas. Its rolled rim is the exception — the tight curve there concentrates light into a continuous hard bright band running all the way around the top of the pan, with a dark band immediately beneath it, and this rim highlight is the brightest thing in the picture. A small embossed marking is pressed into the rim, low in contrast and reading as shape rather than as legible text. They are completely matte and take no highlight. A few still carry a fragment of shell. Broken chocolate chunks scattered among them: each shard has a smooth moulded face that is glossy and reflects light, and freshly fractured faces that are matte, paler and finely granular — that difference between the two faces on the same piece is what makes broken chocolate read as broken rather than cut. Their edges are sharp and angular, and no two pieces are the same shape or size. Around and between them, a scatter of fine ground nut crumb and chocolate dust, denser near the pan and thinning outward, clustered irregularly rather than sprinkled evenly.

LIGHTING — A single hard source placed high and to the right and slightly behind, raking down across the scene. Because it is hard, every element casts a defined shadow: the pan lays a clear shadow across the surface to the left, each falling piece is modelled on one side and dark on the other, and every nut and chocolate shard in the heap casts its own small crisp shadow down and to the left, so the bed reads as a three-dimensional pile rather than a flat texture. The rolled rim of the pan carries the brightest highlight in the frame. The chocolate ribbon's reflections come next. The gelato sits about a stop below them and holds no highlight at all. The background carries a soft brighter wedge on the right where the light spills onto it, falling off to about two stops down at the left edge and the upper left corner. The heaped bed sits about a stop and a half below the gelato. Every transition curves with the surface it crosses; nothing is straight-edged. The lighting sets brightness and falloff only.

BACKGROUND AND SURFACE — A plain deep saturated green backdrop, unbroken, with no seam, texture, object or mark anywhere on it, matte so it holds no sheen. It meets a surface of the same deep green in a soft horizontal transition rather than a hard line. The surface is matte and slightly darker than the backdrop, absorbing light and returning no reflection, so the shadows on it read cleanly. Nothing else is in the frame: no scoop, no cone, no second pan, no cloth, no styling prop. Depth is carried by five separations at five distances: the nearest falling pieces, the front of the heaped bed, the pan, the further falling pieces, and the background.

FOCUS — Depth-of-field blur only, no motion blur anywhere; every edge is a still edge and nothing in the air is streaked. Critical sharpness sits on the near rim of the pan and the front third of the gelato surface — the spatula marks, the air cells, the sharp edges of the chocolate ribbon and its reflections are all fully resolved there. The far end of the pan is slightly soft, and so are the nuts immediately behind it. The nuts and chocolate at the very front of the heap, being closest to the lens, are noticeably soft while their shapes stay completely readable. Among the falling pieces, those at the pan's own distance are sharp, those further back are slightly soft and smaller, and the two or three nearest the lens are clearly out of focus and larger. The background is smooth and entirely off the plane of sharpness.

COLOUR — A single-hue picture with one dark counterpoint. Everything in the frame except the chocolate and the steel is a version of green: the background a deep saturated green, the surface a slightly darker green, the gelato a pale creamy yellow-green, the nut kernels a muted green under mottled purple-tan skins. Against that, the chocolate is a deep near-black brown and is the only dark value in the picture — it must stay brown-black and never drift toward grey or purple. The steel is neutral but picks up the green of its surroundings in its broad reflections while its rim highlight stays neutral white. There is no blue, no orange and no red anywhere in the frame, and the green must stay saturated and clean rather than going grey or olive.

CAPTURE — A real exposure made on a medium-format camera with studio strobe at a short duration. Light falls off toward the four corners, the upper left darkest. The rim highlight on the pan and the brightest points on the chocolate ribbon clip hard and stay narrow; the lit crests of the gelato clip softly and keep their modelling. Shadows stay open — the heaped bed holds readable detail in its shadowed gaps rather than collapsing to black, and the darkest corner of the background sits above pure black. Every repeated element varies: no two nuts the same size, colour or amount of remaining skin, no two chocolate shards the same shape, no two falling pieces at the same angle or the same distance, no two ridges of gelato alike, and none of them evenly spaced. Very slight fine grain throughout, a little heavier in the darker green of the background.

FINAL CHECK — One steel gelato pan, alone, centred and spanning about six tenths of the frame height, its base buried in a heaped bed of nuts and broken chocolate that crosses both side edges of the frame, on a deep green surface against a deep green background with nothing else in the picture. The camera is low, about thirty-five degrees above the surface, so the gelato is seen at a raking angle and the pan is strongly foreshortened. Nuts and chocolate pieces are suspended in the air at different distances, different sizes and different degrees of sharpness, unevenly spread and none touching the pan, all frozen and none streaked. The gelato is completely matte and the chocolate ribbon is glossy — the two must never share the same surface. Do not raise the camera to look down into the pan, do not tidy the heaped bed into an even ring, and do not space the falling pieces evenly.

prompt:

That impossibility is the energy of the picture, and it only works if the suspension is convincing — each piece at a different distance from the lens, at a different angle, at a different size and at a different degree of sharpness, so the eye reads a volume of space around the cup rather than a flat collage of cut-outs pasted around it. The ingredients are also the recipe: every raw component of the drink appears whole in the air, so the viewer reads what is in the cup at a glance. The ground is empty white and pale grey with no context of any kind, so the product is the only content. And the cup itself is transparent, which is the point — the layering inside is the proof of what was blended, and it must be visible.

HERO EFFECT ONE — THE SUSPENSION. The ingredients hang in mid-air, and the picture succeeds or fails on how convincingly they occupy depth. Four rules govern them all. They sit at four clearly different distances from the lens: the furthest are small and slightly soft, the middle ones are at their natural size and critically sharp, and the nearest — the one at the bottom left corner — is noticeably larger than the others and clearly out of focus, with its outline and highlights spread. They are spread unevenly around the cup: some cluster within a hand's width of each other and other areas of the frame are left empty, and none of them sit at equal spacing or on any regular arc. And each casts no shadow on anything and touches nothing, but each is lit from the same direction as the cup, so the light on every piece agrees with the light on the product — this is what stops them reading as pasted cut-outs. Their orientations are plausible for objects in flight: tilted, tumbling, some with their leaves trailing, none standing perfectly upright.

HERO EFFECT TWO — THE DRINK IN THE CUP. Seen through clear plastic, the contents are layered and irregular. The main body is a blended fruit slush: opaque rather than transparent, a deep saturated red-pink, and granular — its surface against the inside wall shows fine pulp texture, tiny paler seed specks scattered through it unevenly, and small trapped air bubbles pressed flat against the plastic. Through that red run pale cream-white streaks, swirled rather than layered flatly, and across the middle third of the cup a band of pale green: thin rounds of cut lime pressed against the inside wall, their segment structure and pale radial membranes visible through the plastic, slightly softened and displaced sideways by the refraction of the wall. Small dark green flecks of crushed leaf are scattered through the paler band. The boundaries between red, cream and green are irregular and marbled, never horizontal lines. Near the top the mixture rises to a slightly domed surface just below the lid. On the outside of the cup, a fine condensation: small separate beads rather than a sheet, denser and larger toward the base and sparse near the rim, each bead a tiny lens with a bright rim, a darker core and one small hard specular on top, varying in size and clustering irregularly.

PROPS AND OBJECTS — The cup is thin clear PET: glossy, so where its curved wall turns away from the lens it concentrates light into two bright vertical bands running the height of the cup, one on each side, and everything seen through it is refracted — shifted and compressed rather than seen through as if it were a window. Its rim is a thicker rolled band that catches a bright continuous line, and its base is a moulded ring that pools a brighter patch of light where it meets the surface. The lid is a clear domed cap snapped over the rim with a ridged flange: the dome is a strong curved reflector, carrying one large soft bright reflection across its upper left and a thinner one on its right, and beneath it sit garnishes — a halved fruit showing its cut face, a wedge of citrus, and a fresh leaf sprig — seen through the plastic slightly softened and slightly displaced. Lime pieces cut to show the interior: the flesh is translucent so light passes through it and the segments glow from within, their membranes reading as pale radial lines, a ring of opaque white pith around them and a thin green rind whose surface is pitted with small oil glands, each pit a tiny shadowed dimple. Mint leaves: saturated green, cupped rather than flat, their upper surface a waxy cuticle laying one broad soft sheen along the leaf, their raised veins branching irregularly and reading darker against the lit lamina, their serrated edges catching thin bright lines. Ice cubes: clear hard-edged blocks, each with sharp bright edges where the light concentrates, internal fracture planes reading as pale sheets inside the block, a cloudier core, and a bright caustic patch where light has been focused through and out the far side — and each cube is slightly different in size and in how far it has begun to round off at its corners. LIGHTING — A large soft source placed high and forward and slightly to the left, plus a second broad fill on the right, so the cup and every floating object are lit from the same directions with soft, open modelling and no hard shadow anywhere. The light passes through the translucent items — the cut citrus, the leaf edges, the ice — so they glow from within and are brighter than the opaque items beside them. The two vertical bands on the cup's wall and the reflection on the dome are the brightest areas on the product. The drink inside sits about a stop below them. Beneath the cup, a soft grey contact shadow spreads across the white surface, darkest and tightest directly under the base and softening quickly outward, anchoring the cup to the table. The background is brightest in a broad pool behind the cup and falls off gently toward the top corners and the upper edges, ending about a stop and a half down. Every transition curves with the surface it crosses; nothing is straight-edged. The lighting sets brightness and falloff only.

BACKGROUND — A plain seamless studio background in a very pale cool grey, curving without a visible edge into a white tabletop, so the transition between them is a soft horizontal gradient rather than a line. The surface is matte with no texture, seam, object or mark anywhere on it. Nothing else is in the frame: no splash, no spill, no straw, no second cup, no garnish resting on the table. Depth is carried by five separations at five distances: the nearest floating item at the bottom left, the mid-distance floating items, the cup, the further floating items, and the background.

FOCUS — Depth-of-field blur only, no motion blur anywhere; every edge is a still edge and no flying object is streaked or dragged. Items further back are slightly soft and slightly smaller. The single item at the bottom left corner is much closer to the lens, noticeably larger, and clearly out of focus, its colour and shape still completely readable. The background is smooth and entirely off the plane of sharpness.

COLOUR — A clean four-value picture. Saturated red in the drink and the whole fruit; saturated fresh green in the leaves, the rinds and the calyxes; clear white in the ice, the pith and the surface; and pale neutral grey in the background. The greys and whites are genuinely neutral and pick up no cast from the fruit around them — that contrast between the saturated food and the neutral ground is what makes the drink read as fresh. There is no blue, no yellow and no warm tint anywhere outside the food.

CAPTURE — A real exposure made on a full-frame camera with studio strobe. Light falls off gently toward the four corners. The bright edges of the ice cubes, the speculars on the condensation beads and the caustics through the citrus clip hard and stay very small; the bands on the cup wall and the reflection on the dome clip softly and keep their shape. prompt:

Take nothing else from image 1 — not its background, not its board or pan, not its surface, not its lighting, not its shadows, not its angle, not its colour grade. The dish is placed into the scene described below and lit by the lights described below.

To change the dish by text instead, replace what is named in the FOOD block, but keep the two rules that make it work. First, every element gets its own optical behaviour: whether it is wet or dry, matte or glossy, whether its cut face differs from its outer surface, and whether it is charred, caramelised or pale. Second, keep the architecture: a loose irregular heap on a dark hot pan, pieces at different angles with some tipped to show their cut faces and some showing only their outsides, never arranged in rows and never evenly spaced.

SWAP SLOT 2 — THE GLASS AND ITS MARK. The beer mug carries a short printed mark on its front. Take the wording, lettering style and colour of that mark from image 1 exactly as printed; the text below never invents any lettering. If no reference is supplied, keep the mark to a single short word in a white script, small and secondary, sitting on the upper third of the glass front. Everything else about the glass — its shape, its frost, the beer and the foam — is built from the text below.

THE PICTURE — A vertical close food and drink photograph taken in a warm dimly lit restaurant: a heap of hot grilled sausage on a black cast-iron plate set into a wooden board, steam rising from it, and beside it a heavily frosted glass beer mug full of pale golden beer with a thick white head, on a dark wooden table, with the room dissolved out of focus behind.

THE READING — This is a bar hero shot and it sells two sensations at once: heat and cold, standing side by side. The steam rising from the pan says the food came out of the kitchen seconds ago. The frost caked on the glass says the beer came out of the freezer. Neither works without the other, and the whole picture exists to put them in the same frame. The camera is low, near the level of the tabletop, so the mug stands tall in profile and the food is seen across its surface rather than from above — a drinker's eye rather than a photographer's. The room behind is present but never resolved: pendant lights, a banquette, tables and chairs, all reduced to warm blur, so the setting is implied and the two lit objects on the table are the only things in focus. And the food is heaped rather than arranged, which is what makes it read as served rather than styled.

FRAMING AND CAMERA — Aspect ratio 4:5, vertical. The mug stands on the right: its body occupies from about six tenths of the frame width to about nine tenths, its handle reaching almost to the right edge, its foam crown at about half the frame height and its base at about nine tenths of the frame height, so it spans roughly the lower half of the picture and is the tallest object in the frame. The wooden board runs in from the left: it crosses the left edge of the frame and continues past it, its far edge at about two thirds of the frame height and its near edge at about nine tenths, and its right end passes behind the mug. The black iron plate sits recessed in the board, and the heap of food on it occupies from about one sixth to about three fifths of the frame width, at about three fifths of the frame height. Behind and left of the food, a napkin holder stands at about one quarter of the frame width and half the frame height. Steam rises from the food through the upper middle of the frame. Everything above the far edge of the table — roughly the upper half of the picture — is the out-of-focus room. Lens 85mm, camera low, about twenty degrees above the plane of the tabletop, so the mug is seen almost in profile and the food is seen across its surface. Aperture f/2.8.

HERO EFFECT ONE — THE BEER AND THE FROSTED GLASS. Three separate materials stacked in one object, and each behaves differently.

The frost is the outermost layer: a fine crystalline bloom covering the outside of the glass, matte and light-scattering so it reads as an opaque white veil rather than as transparency. It is thickest and whitest around the base and along the handle, thins as it rises, and is patchier near the rim. Where it is thick, the beer behind it is not seen directly but glows through it as a soft diffused amber; where it is thin, the liquid shows more clearly. Running down through the frost are a few clear tracks and larger condensation droplets, each droplet a small lens with a bright rim, a darker core and one hard white specular on its upper side, and they vary in size and cluster irregularly rather than sitting in an even array.

The beer inside is a pale transparent gold and it glows because light passes through it: it is lighter and brighter where the path through the liquid is shortest, near the outer curve of the glass, and deepens toward a richer amber through the thickest part. Rising through it are strings of small bubbles, released from a few separate points on the inner wall rather than from everywhere at once, so they form three or four distinct rising columns; the bubbles grow slightly larger as they rise and the columns wander rather than running straight. The glass is moulded with vertical panels around its lower body, and each panel catches its own separate reflection and its own edge of concentrated light, so the base of the mug reads as a set of bright vertical bands. The thick base acts as a lens, pooling a brighter patch of light just above the tabletop.

The head is the third material: a dense white foam standing proud above the rim in a slightly domed crown, taller at the back than the front. Its surface is not smooth — it is finely cratered and irregular, made of tiny bubbles packed together, with slightly larger bubbles around its outer edge where it meets the glass, and one or two shallow dips in its surface. It clings to the inside of the glass in a thin ring just below the rim. It is the brightest and the only pure white thing in the picture, and it must clip softly and keep its texture rather than blowing out into a flat white shape.

HERO EFFECT TWO — THE STEAM. Thin pale vapour rising from the hot food, and the rule that governs it is this: steam is only visible where it passes in front of something dark. Against the dark banquette and the shadowed parts of the room it reads clearly as pale grey-white; where it drifts across a bright area of the background it disappears almost completely, and it must not be drawn as a solid shape floating over everything. It leaves the food as two or three separate narrow threads, denser and slightly more opaque close to the pan, and rises about a third of the frame height, curling and folding over itself, splitting into finer strands, wavering sideways rather than going straight up, and thinning to nothing near the top. Its edges are soft and feathered everywhere. It is frozen by the exposure — it holds internal curl and structure and is not dragged or streaked in any direction — and it never obscures the food beneath it or crosses the mug.

FOOD — A loose heap of grilled sausage cut into thick diagonal slices and short chunks, piled unevenly with some pieces tipped to show their cut faces and others showing only their curved outsides, some resting on top of others and the heap higher at one side than the other. The cut faces show a coarse interior in warm pink-red with irregular white flecks of fat scattered through it, and their outer edges are browned and caramelised to a deeper red-brown. The casing on the outside is shrunken and slightly wrinkled, taut over the meat, darker than the interior, with a few near-black char marks where it touched the hottest metal — irregular in size and placement, never evenly distributed. Every piece is wet with rendered fat, so each returns a broad soft sheen along its curve plus one or two small hard speculars where the fat has pooled, and a little clear fat has run down onto the plate and glistens there. A scattering of coarse salt sits on some pieces and not others.

PROPS AND OBJECTS — A rectangular cast-iron plate, matte black with a slightly pebbled seasoned surface that scatters light so it returns only a broad dull sheen along its raised rim and no highlight anywhere on its face, its two handle lugs visible at the left end. It sits recessed into a thick wooden serving board in honey-toned oak: the wood is smooth and finished satin, its grain running in long straight lines with a few darker streaks, its edges rounded and catching a soft continuous line of light, with a routed slot at one end. Behind and left of the food, a small metal wire napkin holder with white folded paper napkins standing in it as a triangle: the paper is completely matte, takes no shine, and is the brightest neutral surface in the left half of the frame, and the thin metal of the holder catches two or three narrow bright lines. Beneath everything, a table of dark stained wood with a satin finish, returning a soft broad reflection of the mug's base and a dim pool beneath the board rather than a sharp mirror image, with a diffuse contact shadow directly under the mug and under the board so nothing floats.

And the room's own warm practical lights in the background, which own the amber glow behind and light nothing on the table. The foam is the brightest thing in the frame; the beer sits about a stop below it; the food about a stop and a half below that; the iron plate about three stops down and the table about three and a half, with the darkest corners of the room around four.
